title: Stove Auto Shut-Off Devices: How They Work, What They Cost and What They Can't Do
subtitle: A plain-English look at plug-in add-ons that cut power or gas to a forgotten stove, and the questions to ask before you buy one.
excerpt: A stove shut-off device can turn off a burner someone forgot about, but only under certain conditions. Here is how the main types work, what the makers say they cost, and where they fall short.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Most of us have done it at least once. You put a pot on to simmer, the phone rings, and twenty minutes later you smell something burning. For an older parent who lives alone, or who is starting to forget small steps, that moment can worry the whole family.

Stove auto shut-off devices are one answer. They are add-ons that connect to a stove's power or gas and act on a specific trigger, such as a smoke alarm sounding. They do not replace a watchful eye, but they can act as a backstop. One note on sources: the details below come from the makers' own product pages. We have not tested these devices, and we did not find independent reviews to check them against.
There are two main approaches, and they differ in what triggers the shut-off.
Devices that listen for the smoke alarm

FireAvert's devices sit behind the stove and wait for your household smoke alarm to go off. In the maker's words, the unit "continuously listens for your smoke alarm." After an alarm, it waits 30 seconds, which the maker says allows you to clear minor cooking smoke. If the alarm keeps sounding, it cuts power to an electric stove, or closes the gas valve on a gas stove. It can also send a text or app alert to a phone.
Devices that notice you left the kitchen

iGuard takes a different route. It detects when the cook has left the kitchen, alerts them, and then turns the stove off. Its maker says this forgotten-cooking protection works without Wi-Fi (a home's wireless internet connection). The maker's page does not say whether the app features need Wi-Fi, so ask before you buy. The app offers monitoring, remote shutoff "where supported," and lock and schedule controls. There is also an extended timer for slow simmering.

It is worth being clear-eyed here. A smoke-triggered device only acts once there is enough smoke to set off the alarm. A hot pan that is not smoking yet will not trigger it. If the smoke alarm is dead or out of earshot of the device, nothing happens. The 30-second wait is on purpose, so it cannot stop a grease fire that flares up faster than that.

None of these devices puts out a fire. Cutting the heat is not the same as having a person in the room. For someone living with dementia or memory concerns, a shut-off is a backup, not a substitute for supervision, and it is worth talking with their doctor about what kind of cooking help is safe. In an emergency, call 911.

items: Match the stove type. Electric and gas models are different products. Check which one you have before ordering.

Match the plug. Electric stoves use a 3-prong or 4-prong plug. Look behind the stove and note the prongs and cord color. iGuard, for example, lists a 4-prong plug (NEMA 14-50, black cord) and a 3-prong plug (NEMA 10-50, grey cord).

Ask about gas installation. Gas versions connect to the gas line, which reviewers on FireAvert's page call the hard part. One suggests a professional, which could add a plumber's fee. Check with your local fire department or gas utility about gas line work.

Ask about ongoing fees. FireAvert lists "0 monthly fees" for app alerts, but its page also mentions a monitoring plan with no price shown. Confirm what that plan costs. iGuard's page shows no monthly fee.
Count the full cost. Prices on these pages run from about $250 to $550 or more, far above a simple $15 kitchen timer.
Check Wi-Fi and phone needs. Alerts and dashboards need Wi-Fi and a smartphone.
Confirm stock and shipping. As general advice, ask when an item will ship and what the return policy is before paying.

Think about access. These devices sit behind the stove, and the plug can be hard to reach. If no one can get to it easily, a device may not suit your kitchen. FireAvert says it can be reset from a phone.

sections.content: A note on price and stock, as shown on the makers' pages in October 2026. FireAvert's electric and gas pages both showed "Sold out" text next to an "Add to cart" button. The 4-prong electric version's $249.99 price comes from FireAvert's collection page, not its own product page. The iGuard page showed both $549 and "$699 total – Shipping Extra," and listed stock as "Inventory coming in monthly." That is why we give no single price for it.
Setting it up and using it well

Start with the smoke alarms, especially if you choose a smoke-triggered model. Test the alarm nearest the kitchen, replace weak batteries, and make sure the device can hear it. A smoke-triggered device is only as good as the alarm it listens to.

iGuard says its electric model installs with no electrician. For a gas stove, reviewers suggest a professional, so ask a qualified person rather than working on the gas line yourself. Because the gas version also closes the valve on any power loss, expect that an outage may shut off the gas, which can be a nuisance.

Once it is in, set up phone alerts for whoever is most likely to check in, such as an adult child or a nearby neighbor. Then talk it over with the person who cooks. Explain what the device does, what the 30-second pause means, and what to do if the stove suddenly goes off.

If you rent, ask your landlord before buying. These devices change how the stove connects to power or gas, and some leases do not allow that. These add-ons also do not suit a parent who needs someone present while cooking.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A stove shut-off will not make a kitchen fireproof, and it works only in the situations described above. Paired with working smoke alarms and regular check-ins, it can be one reasonable layer of safety to consider.
